prompt: In `ls -l` output, what does a leading 'l' in the first column indicate?
options: A symbolic link
A regular file with a long name
A locked file
A block device
explanation: The first character encodes the file type: - regular, d directory, l symbolic link, c character device, b block device, p named pipe, s socket. A symlink line also shows an arrow (->) to its target.

prompt: For a device file, what do the major and minor numbers identify?
options: Major identifies the device driver; minor identifies the specific device or partition
Major identifies the device size; minor identifies its speed
Major is the inode number; minor is the link count
Major identifies the mount point; minor the file system type
explanation: A driver gets a unique major number — 8 for SCSI/SATA disks, 253 for device mapper, 11 for optical — and each device or partition that driver manages gets its own minor number. They appear in the size columns of ls -l for device files.

prompt: How do the `file` and `stat` commands differ when run against /etc/sysconfig/anaconda?
options: file reports the kind of content (ASCII text); stat reports the file type (regular file)
file reports the size; stat reports the permissions
They produce identical output
file works only on binaries; stat only on text
explanation: file inspects content and names it specifically (e.g. 'ASCII text'), while stat reports the metadata including the generic type 'regular file'. Linux does not use filename extensions to determine type.

prompt: How do gzip and bzip2 compare?
options: bzip2 usually compresses better but runs slower than gzip
gzip usually compresses better but runs slower than bzip2
They produce identical output at identical speed
bzip2 only works on directories
explanation: bzip2 typically achieves a smaller result at the cost of speed. The difference matters on large files; for small ones either is fine. gzip appends .gz and bzip2 appends .bz2, replacing the original file in both cases.

prompt: Compress the file ~/fstab with gzip.
explanation: gzip replaces fstab with fstab.gz. gunzip fstab.gz reverses it, restoring the original name, size and timestamp. gzip -l shows compression statistics, and -r walks a directory tree.

prompt: Create a gzip-compressed tarball /tmp/skel.tar.gz containing the /etc/skel directory.
explanation: -c creates, -z pipes through gzip, -v is verbose, and -f names the archive. Use -j instead of -z for bzip2. The archive stores paths without the leading slash so it can be extracted anywhere.

prompt: List the contents of /tmp/skel.tar.gz without extracting it.
explanation: -t lists the archive table of contents. Modern tar detects the compression automatically, but naming it with -z is always safe.

prompt: Extract the bzip2-compressed archive /tmp/skel.tar.bz2 into /tmp rather than the current directory.
explanation: -x extracts, -j selects bzip2, and -C changes to the target directory before extracting. Note the case distinction: lowercase -c creates an archive, uppercase -C changes directory.

prompt: Which statements about tar are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: -r appends files to an existing uncompressed tarball
-p preserves permissions and should be given when a normal user creates an archive
tar can preserve SELinux contexts and ownership
-r and -u work on gzip-compressed tarballs
-x creates the archive
explanation: -r and -u cannot append to a compressed tarball — only to an uncompressed one. -x extracts; -c creates. tar does preserve ownership, timestamps and extended attributes such as SELinux contexts.

topic: Edit Text Files using the vim Editor
prompt: Which vim command opens a new line below the current one and switches to insert mode?
options: o
O
a
I
explanation: Lowercase o opens a line below; uppercase O opens one above. i inserts before the cursor, I at the start of the line, a after the cursor, and A at the end of the line.

topic: Edit Text Files using the vim Editor
prompt: In vim, what does `:%s/profile/Profile/g` do?
options: Replaces every occurrence of profile with Profile throughout the file
Replaces only the first occurrence on each line
Replaces occurrences only on the current line
Searches for profile without replacing anything
explanation: % applies the substitution to every line and the trailing /g makes it replace all occurrences per line. Without /g, only the first match on each line is replaced. :u undoes a last-line-mode command.

topic: Edit Text Files using the vim Editor
prompt: Which vim commands write the file to disk? (Select all that apply.)
options: :w
:wq
:x
:set nu
explanation: :w writes without quitting, :wq writes and quits, and :x is the common equivalent of :wq. :q! quits and discards changes, while :set nu only toggles on-screen line numbering (never saved into the file).

topic: Edit Text Files using the vim Editor
prompt: In vim command mode, what does `3dd` do?
options: Deletes the current line and the two below it
Deletes the third line of the file
Deletes three characters
Duplicates the current line three times
explanation: Most command-mode operations accept a leading repeat count, so 3dd deletes three lines starting at the cursor. Likewise 2yy yanks two lines and 2p pastes twice. Last-line-mode commands like :6,12d do not take a repeat prefix.

topic: Perform Essential File and Directory Operations
prompt: Create the nested directory hierarchy dir2/perl/perl5 in one command, creating any missing parent directories.
explanation: -p creates intermediate parent directories as needed and does not error if they already exist. Add -v to have mkdir report what it created.

topic: Perform Essential File and Directory Operations
prompt: Why does `cp` prompt root before overwriting a file, but not a normal user?
options: A predefined alias adds -i for the root user
Root's umask forces interactive mode
cp always prompts; normal users simply do not see it
The kernel enforces confirmation for UID 0
explanation: Root's shell environment aliases cp, mv and rm to include -i. For a normal user the copy silently overwrites unless -i is given explicitly.

topic: Perform Essential File and Directory Operations
prompt: Copy file1 into /tmp keeping its original timestamp, permissions and ownership.
explanation: -p preserves the attributes. Use -r (or -R) to copy a directory tree, and -i to be prompted before overwriting.

topic: Perform Essential File and Directory Operations
prompt: A file literally named * exists in /tmp. Which command removes only that file?
options: rm /tmp/\*
rm /tmp/*
rm -r /tmp/*
rmdir /tmp/*
explanation: The backslash escapes the asterisk so the shell passes it literally instead of expanding it. `rm /tmp/*` would glob and delete every file in /tmp — an expensive mistake with root privileges.

topic: Perform Essential File and Directory Operations
prompt: Which command monitors /var/log/messages as new entries are written to it?
options: tail -f /var/log/messages
head -f /var/log/messages
cat -f /var/log/messages
less -n /var/log/messages
explanation: tail -f follows the file and prints new lines as they arrive; Ctrl+c stops it. tail shows the last ten lines by default and head the first ten.

prompt: Create a soft link named soft10 that points to the file file10 in the current directory.
explanation: -s makes a symbolic link. Without -s, ln creates a hard link instead — a second name for the same inode.

prompt: Which statements about hard links are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: All hard-linked names share one inode and identical metadata
Creating one increases the target's link count
They cannot cross file system boundaries
They can be created for directories
They store the pathname of the target
explanation: Hard links to directories are not permitted, and it is soft links that store a pathname. A hard link is simply another filename mapped to the same inode, so the data survives until the link count reaches zero.

prompt: What happens to a symbolic link when its target file is deleted?
options: The link remains but now points to a non-existent file
The link is deleted automatically
The link's data is preserved because it holds a copy
The target cannot be deleted while a symlink exists
explanation: A symlink holds only the target's pathname in its own inode, so deleting the target leaves a dangling link. Deleting the symlink, by contrast, has no effect on the target.

prompt: You need several names for one file so that editing through any name changes the same data. Copy or link?
options: Link — all links reference the same underlying data
Copy — copies stay synchronised automatically
Copy with -p, which keeps the inode
Either; they behave identically
explanation: A copy duplicates the data at a new location with its own inode, so edits diverge. A link is an additional reference to the same data, which is what you want when the names must stay in sync.
